A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Cascadia. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching across revisions, relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPU-serving experiments, including DeepSeek and Llama comparisons, throughput and SLO measurements, deployment case studies, ablations and scheduler runtimes.

after.justification: V2 retains original serving experiments and additionally reports simulator validation, fluctuating-workload evaluation and comparisons with Sarathi-Serve.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces weighted Tchebycheff scalarization and weight sweeping to generate a Pareto front with latency minimization plus a normalized penalty for violating a specified quality requirement. Appendix C supplies the corresponding latency-budget variant. This substantially revises routing optimization while retaining threshold-based cascades and MILP deployment.

E1.justification: V2 adds an evaluated nonstationary serving scenario in which workloads transition through traces 1, 2 and 3. The underlying MT-Bench coverage and application domains remain unchanged; this extends input-environment coverage using the existing traces.

E2.justification: V2 adds an actual Sarathi-Serve comparison on traces 1–3 at quality requirement 90 (Appendix F, Table 4). The existing SGLang-served standalone models and CascadeServe comparisons remain. The DeepSeek-dist naming clarifies retained models rather than introducing another comparator.

E3.justification: The scheduler scaling sweep changes from 32/64/128 GPUs to 16/32/48/64/80 GPUs. Added protocols include 8/16/10-minute workload segments and simulator validation across seven parallelism configurations with average input/output lengths of 1600/16. The stated resampling example also changes from 100 requests every 10 minutes to 50 every 5 minutes.

E4.justification: V2 tests whether rescheduling remains effective under changing workloads and whether simulator throughput predictions agree with measurements (Section 4.4 and Appendix B). V1's empirical Pareto-search analysis and Figure 13 are removed. Existing allocation/parallelism ablations and deployment case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2's simulator absolute percentage errors quantify prediction accuracy, without introducing statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds Sarathi-Serve speedups of 1.322, 1.953 and 1.611 (Table 4), simulator errors of 1.64–7.69% (Table 1), and fluctuating-workload results (Figure 11). Scheduler runtimes are revised, including completion within 20 seconds at 32 GPUs versus within one minute in v1, alongside optimizer and setting changes. Main DeepSeek/Llama benchmarks and ablations retain their results; Pareto-search results disappear.

T1.justification: V2 redefines the optimization anchors as best/worst quality, replaces the weighted minimax objective with a normalized constraint-violation penalty, and states a quality-feasibility property for sufficiently large penalties. Appendices C and D add explicit latency-constrained and coupled bi-level formulations. These change the mathematical objectives and stated properties.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of jointly optimizing routing, resource allocation and parallelism for quality-preserving LLM serving. Headline advantages remain up to 4× tighter latency SLOs and 5× throughput, with the same 2.3× and 2.4× averages.

C2.justification: V1's limitations concerning LLM-specific applicability, the 32-GPU experimental scale and homogeneous hardware are removed rather than relocated. V2 adds interpretations that simulator accuracy is sufficient for configuration selection and that online adaptation preserves throughput benefits despite scheduling overhead.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents simulator dispatching, queues, batching, offline profiling and parallelism modeling, plus quality profiling, routing initialization and stopping, included judging overhead, and Sarathi-Serve implementation/tuning. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to every described component. Conversely, the Scratchpad repository URL present in v1 is omitted.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations on unified routing/cascading, TurboMind and parallel training, and removes the BurstGPT citation. Central positioning against existing cascade-serving systems remains. The speculative-decoding/early-exit discussion is relocated to Appendix A; the FlashFlex/HexiScale references identify the same arXiv work.

P1.justification: The central scheduling exposition is substantially rewritten around deployment and routing solvers, with a revised worked example and expanded procedural explanations. V2 removes the RQ1–RQ3 framing, relocates related-work material and reorganizes the appendices. The title, author list and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: V2 changes typography and page layout, replaces the workflow diagram with Algorithm 1, removes Pareto illustrations, and adds validation/comparison tables and a fluctuating-workload plot. The main SLO grid changes from three rows by four columns to two by six. Existing case-study tables move to Appendix E.

improvement.justification: The simulator documentation and measured validation, online workload test, and tuned Sarathi-Serve comparison improve reproducibility and empirical support beyond v1. However, explicit applicability limitations are lost, and presentation inaccuracies remain, including Figure 5's obsolete row/column description after rearrangement. The additions provide a meaningful but limited net quality improvement.
